content: Cultural references to stuttering have been depicted in various forms of media, literature, film, television, and music, often reflecting societal attitudes and perceptions of the condition. Literature Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, was denied the opportunity to become a priest due to his stuttering. In response, he wrote a poem that humorously addresses stuttering, including lines such as: Learn well your grammar / And never stammer. Carroll’s stuttering is subtly referenced in Alice in Wonderland through the character of the Dodo bird, which is said to resemble Carroll himself. This connection is highlighted by the fact that Carroll often pronounced his last name as Do-Do-Dodgson. Film The 1988 film A Fish Called Wanda features a character with a severe stutter, played by Michael Palin. The character is portrayed as socially awkward and reclusive, embodying common stereotypes about stutterers. The film explores a range of reactions to stuttering, from sympathy to indifference to outright cruelty. While some viewers criticized the film for its portrayal of the character as a victim of bullying, others appreciated its honest depiction of the challenges faced by people who stutter. Palin, whose father also stuttered, used the role to raise awareness and later founded the Michael Palin Centre for Stammering Children in London. In The Right Stuff (1983), the stuttering of John Glenn’s wife, Annie, is depicted as a source of personal struggle. Her fear of public speaking due to her stutter is shown during Glenn’s spaceflight. Over time, Annie underwent intensive speech therapy and successfully managed her stuttering, later delivering a public speech about her experiences. One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest features Billy Bibbit, a character whose pronounced stutter significantly impacts his self-esteem. His stutter is linked to traumatic experiences, including a failed marriage proposal. In the story, his stutter temporarily disappears after a transformative experience but ultimately reflects the deep psychological scars he carries. The film Rocket Science centers on Hal Hefner, a teenager with a stutter, while M. Night Shyamalan’s Lady in the Water (2006) features a character whose stutter selectively disappears in certain interactions. In Stephen King’s IT, the character Bill Denbrough stutters more severely when under stress or fear, with his speech impediment symbolically tied to his emotional state. Television Porky Pig, a well-known animated character from Looney Tunes, is characterized by his stutter, which was originally voiced by a real stutterer before being taken over by Mel Blanc. In 1991, the National Stuttering Project protested the portrayal of Porky Pig, leading Warner Bros. to support anti-bullying campaigns and donate to the Stuttering Foundation of America. An episode of MASH features a stuttering soldier who is ridiculed by his peers but ultimately shown to be highly intelligent. The storyline highlights the misconceptions about stuttering and includes a subplot revealing that Major Winchester’s sister also stutters. In Open All Hours, Ronnie Barker’s character has a stutter that often leads to humorous situations, while Nicholas Brendon, who played Xander Harris on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, overcame his stutter and became a spokesperson for the Stuttering Foundation of America. On South Park, the character Jimmy Vulmer has a severe stutter, which is often used for comedic effect. Music The 1918 song K-K-K-Katy by Geoffrey O’Hara became a wartime hit, using stuttered lyrics to portray a bashful suitor. Alvin Lucier’s experimental piece I Am Sitting in a Room incorporates his own stuttering as part of the composition, aiming to smooth out speech irregularities through repetition. Stuttering has been used as a stylistic device in popular music. Buddy Holly, The Who (in My Generation), and Bachman-Turner Overdrive (in You Ain’t Seen Nothing Yet) all employed stuttering effects in their songs. In some cases, these effects were initially unintentional but became iconic elements of the music. Scatman John turned his stutter into a unique musical style, blending scat singing with inspirational lyrics aimed at empowering stutterers. His hit song Scatman became a global success. Other examples include Placebo’s use of a stammering voice in their song Swallow and Teddy Geiger’s For You I Will (Confidence), which references stuttering in its lyrics. Bloc Party’s lead singer, Kele Okereke, has a pronounced stutter when speaking but not while singing. Radio John Melendez, known as Stuttering John, became a prominent figure on Howard Stern’s radio show despite his stutter. His role involved conducting celebrity interviews, and his speech impediment was both a source of humor and a defining characteristic. Stern’s show also featured other individuals with speech impediments, who were embraced by the audience despite their conditions being used for comedic purposes. These examples illustrate the diverse ways in which stuttering has been represented in cultural contexts, ranging from ridicule and stereotypes to empowerment and advocacy.
